source.title: Neuron-Level Emotion Control in Speech-Generative Large Audio-Language Models
source.authors: Xiu-Tian Zhao; I. R. Ulgen; Philipp Koehn; Björn W. Schuller; Berrak Sisman

record.tranche_reason: The study uses activation-based neuron selection and intervention to control speech emotion, but does not test the claim versions about neuron job interpretability, audit shares, attribution graphs, or automated explanation scores.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on emotion control through selected neurons. Those findings concern a related but different question from the listed versions: it does not assess whether neuron poles have one or more understandable jobs, or whether explanations predict where neurons activate. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study selects emotion-sensitive MLP gate neurons in three speech-generative audio-language models and steers them to control emotional voice conversion. It reports only its own pipeline's performance: emotion match, WER, UTMOS, human preference and layer localization. It never audits whether neurons or poles have one main job (V1, V2). It never studies InceptionV1 or superposition (V3), tools or architecture versus interpretable share (V4), attribution graphs (V5), or explanation-versus-activation prediction (V6, V7). The neuron-level framing is used as a tool, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that identification requires success-filtered aggregation, and that CAS and MAD selectors beat LAP and LAPE. They say effects transfer to unseen speakers (emotion-dependent) and are corroborated by human listening (62% win). They attribute the high-strength WER rise to semantic drift rather than loss of intelligibility.
record.recipe_differences: This is an activation-based emotion-control study in speech-generative audio-language models, using success-filtered neuron selection and inference-time interventions; it is not a pole-job audit or an attribution-graph evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report sensitivity to selector, mask sparsity, success-set size, intervention method and strength, evaluation judge, module, target emotion, and seen versus unseen speakers.

fits_no_version.finding: Emotion-control signal is distributed rather than ultra-sparse. Too small a mask (r=0.1%) gives weak effects; larger masks (r=1%) add cross-emotion spillover.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emotion control in speech LALMs relies on distributed neuron sets, not single dedicated neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron sets identified from human-filtered and SER-filtered successes overlap only partially (mean Jaccard 0.118), though their layer distributions match (JSD 0.021).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which individual neurons get identified as emotion-sensitive depends on the supervision signal, while their layer locus is stable.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering CAS-selected neurons in language-model decoder MLPs raises target-emotion match, with a WER cost at high strength; synthesis-module interventions are inert.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emotion-control units in speech LALMs are actionable in intermediate-to-late LM-side MLP layers.

record.problems: The study evaluates a specific speech-generation task and emotion-control measure, not whether neurons have human-readable main jobs. Several detailed results are presented only in figures without numerical values in the text. Table results generally do not report uncertainty intervals; confidence intervals are mentioned for Figure 10.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's per-selector cross-effect and UTMOS results in Table 3, selector-specific WER values other than the noted CAS cases, detailed emotion-by-emotion heatmap values in Figures 3–7, and the neuron-set overlap statistics in Table 5 were not separately extracted. These results concern emotion-control tuning or identification agreement, not the listed claim versions. The plotted numeric values for Figures 4–7, 9, and 10 are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: No pole-level audit of one-job, two-job or not-understood shares; Qwen3-32B is not studied.
No job-share audit across dense or MoE models or across scale.
No InceptionV1, pose features or superposition analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization or tools versus interpretable share.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No test of explanations against where neurons fire.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is a speech-emotion steering study with no bearing on neuron-interpretability shares or explanation scoring. No verdicts are given. Selector-comparison rows (LAP, LAPE, MAD, random) are the study's own method variants.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate Qwen3-32B pole-level shares of one-job, two-job, or not-understood neurons.
Does not audit job shares across model scale, dense or MoE architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
Does not study InceptionV1 examples, pose features, recursive generalization, or superposition.
Does not test whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain interpretability rates, or estimate such rates for vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or evaluate their behavioral explanation or reconstruction error.
Does not test explanations against activation locations on held-out examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
